extracted.intended_audience: NLP and computer-vision researchers working on computational humor, benchmark developers, and multimodal ML practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Benchmarks and evaluation tasks derived from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest for measuring progressively sophisticated aspects of computational humor understanding (matching captions to cartoons, selecting winning captions, and explaining why captions are funny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching a joke to a cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching a joke to a cartoon (task derived from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This task evaluates whether models can select the correct caption for a given cartoon image; reported performance gaps include best multimodal models falling ~30 accuracy points behind human performance on this matching task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying a winning caption
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying a winning caption (selecting which caption won the contest for a cartoon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates models' ability to predict contest-winning captions among candidate captions, capturing preference/selection judgments beyond simple semantic fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining why a winning caption is funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining why a winning caption is funny (producing an explanation for the humor of a winning caption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a higher-level task measuring explanatory understanding of humor; human-authored explanations are used as reference and human preference tests show human explanations preferred head-to-head over best machine-authored ones (few-shot GPT-4) in more than two-thirds of cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal vs language-only evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare multimodal models (challenged with cartoon images directly) and language-only models (given multifaceted descriptions of the visual scene to simulate human-level visual understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows assessment of whether failures stem from visual understanding or higher-level humor reasoning; language-only condition uses ground-truth visual scene descriptors to isolate non-visual aspects of humor understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotations describing visual scene and unusual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Release and use of annotations describing the image's locations/entities, what's unusual in the scene, and an explanation of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These annotations serve both as inputs for language-only models (scene descriptors) and as structured supervision/evaluation signals for models attempting to capture the elements relevant to humor (e.g., unusualness, entities, spatial relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive sophistication of tasks / key elements of cartoon humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks encapsulate progressively more sophisticated aspects of 'understanding' a cartoon; key elements include the complex, often surprising relationships between images and captions and the frequent inclusion of indirect and playful allusions to human experience and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should account for image-caption relational complexity and cultural/indirect allusion comprehension; success metrics must reflect models' abilities on both surface-level fit and deeper pragmatic/cultural reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaderboard and released resources for benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Release of models, code, leaderboard, and corpus to support benchmarking on these humor-understanding tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided leaderboard and released corpus to compare systems consistently; the paper reports baselines and human performance for reference.
